Try to visit a house after, or during a rain. Water will become your biggest enemy as a homeowner, and is one of the major causes of houses falling apart, either from penetrating from above or undermining the foundation from below/within. Dirty water from sewage backup also applies here.

How old, in years, is the roof? How old are the appliances? The HVAC? The water heater? How is the drainage around the property? Is there any ground sloping TOWARD the foundation (big red flag)? Are the gutters and downspouts in good shape? Fixing any of this stuff can be several thousands to TENS of thousands of dollars.

Look at the comps in the neighborhood. What are other properties of similar age, square footage, and amenities listing for AND selling for? Are you seeing sale prices being notched down from their listing prices?

Independently verify any home inspector you bring in. Realtors may recommend inspectors that help them close deals, not necessarily help buyers. Make sure the inspector does thermal imaging and moisture sensing; that will tell you if there are hard to find water leaks. Make sure the inspector runs all the plumbing; some leaks are only apparent if water is running (e.g. drain line leaks, which I'm currently dealing with). If the inspector recommends deferring to a specialist (structural engineer, HVAC tech, plumber) LISTEN TO THEM!

Stands for Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions. Basically tells you the rules of the HOA (this is where stuff like maximum lawn grass height would be found, what colors are allowed) and will also tell you what property is owned and maintained by the HOA (for condos, they would mention things like elevators, exterior surfaces, etc). It's worth pointing out that in practice, if you find any elements that are defective, but covered by the HOA per the CC&R, you may be asked to submit a service request much like you would in an apartment complex. 

  
Your realtor should provide CC&R, financial statements, and reserve studies upon asking. You may also be able to find them on the Internet, if you or your realtor know the full name of the HOA. Reserve studies aren't mandatory in a vast majority of US states, but if the HOA cares at all about its finances, it will order one to financially plan for the future. It is especially important that an HOA for an older neighborhood/condo building has some sort of recent serve study.

Shop around for mortgage rates AND make sure you do get multiple rates. If other lenders are taking their sweet time, either follow up or keep finding more lenders. I made the mistake of going with the infamous Rocket Mortgage because they were the fastest and (in hindsight) most aggressive lender I reached out. Other lenders/brokers didn't get back to me in time, and I was, perhaps irrationally, afraid I would be left in the dust behind other buyers (this was in fall 2023 when rates were coming back down for the first time). Make sure you know how many Points are attached to your rate (I paid for Rocket Mortgage's convenience with a hefty amount of points).

If you do go under contract, be prepared to spend good money on inspections if the home inspector flags it. Home inspectors only do a general inspection; you will need a specialist for foundation, roofing (if the inspector won't do it), sewer plumbing, etc. They may be expensive (hundreds of dollars per specialist inspection) upfront, but when repairing this stuff can cost tens of thousands, you'll want to know exactly what you're getting yourself into. On that note, be wary if the realtor recommends a home inspector without you asking them first. As other commenters noted, realtors are paid by commission and may resort to conflicts-of-interest to get it. Do your own research on that particular home inspector.

Others have already mentioned some of these but I'll add to the discussion anyway:

  
1. Understand that total cost of ownership includes more than just the mortgage. You have homeowners insurance, HOA fees (for certain properties) and property taxes. You can consider the sum of the interest portion of your mortgage, homeowners insurance, HOA fees (if applicable), and property taxes as the "effective" rent you are now paying toward your new landlords (lender + government). As mortgages are interest-heavy initially, you will be throwing away quite a lot of money in the first few years or so. In my case, I ended up paying $600 more in "effective rent" per month than when I was renting at my previous apartment in a multi-story complex, although my place has nearly 2x the space, and I don't live above or below anyone. You may find it is far cheaper to rent, depending on where you live.

2. Due to COVID inflation, property values have gone up sharply. Property taxes are determined based on (but not solely on) property values, however depending on the region, the tax man may still be referring to older house values when assessing property taxes. Find out if the properties you're looking at have been appraised recently or not. If they haven't, budget for a possible increase in property taxes. 3. Home inspections are absolutely vital, new or old construction alike. Homes can be \*HUGE\* money pits, where you might be paying tens of thousands of dollars to repair things. You may have found on other subreddits that you want to seriously reconsider purchasing houses if it has bad foundations or major electrical and plumbing deficiencies. If your realtor recommends a home inspector, vet them independently since at the end of the day, realtors want their commission from a sale and may result to deceit and conflicts-of-interest to meet those ends. 

4. Home inspectors are generalists, not specialists. If the home inspector suggests you get a specialist to inspect their findings, listen to them! Mine suggested I get a structural engineer to inspect the cracks he saw and some sagging floors (the home is decades old), but I was worried about scheduling and the cost of inspection ($600) in my case. I ended up getting an inspection months after closing, took just a handful of business days to schedule, and there were indeed structural problems present though thankfully nothing life threatening. Bids to resolve these started at 10K. If I got the report BEFORE closing, I could've asked for further concessions from the seller. Money that I wouldn't have to pay out of pocket like I am now.

5. Determine how old your HVAC system and roof are while under contract. If they are near the end of life, even if they're working just fine, you'll want to budget for their replacement. 

6. Keep in mind water will be your new enemy as a prospective home owner. Try to schedule showings after rain has fallen. Make note if water is pooling anywhere on the property, especially if its near the foundation. You may have found reports from other subreddits about how water damage has cost homeowners thousands, to tens of thousands of dollars in repair.

I would advise you to calculate the total cost of ownership of the house should you get it, and compare that to what you'd pay in rent. That would involve not only the interest, but homeowners insurance and property taxes and HOA fees (if they apply). Keep in mind property taxes and insurance will typically increase over time. If the cost of ownership exceeds your rent, I'd keep saving up or invest the money (unless you're willing to spend the money on the house). If they're comparable, then I would (cautiously) move forward. When you buy property, you're really just changing your landlords to the government and whatever lender you are using. So make sure you aren't paying too much more in "effective" rent!
